title: Flat Tire Repair
summary: Remove the wheel, find and fix the puncture, and get rolling again.

steps.instruction: Shift to the smallest rear cog/chainring combo to slacken the chain, then remove the wheel. If it's a hub-motor wheel, disconnect the motor cable connector first.
Fully deflate the tire, then work one side of the tire bead off the rim with tire levers, starting opposite the valve.
Pull out the inner tube, leaving the other side of the tire still seated on the rim.
Inspect the inside of the tire for the object that caused the puncture (thorn, glass, wire) and remove it. Run a finger carefully around the inside to check for other sharp edges.
Patch the tube (rough up the area, apply patch cement, press the patch on and hold) or swap in a new/spare tube.
Partially inflate the tube just enough to hold its shape, tuck it inside the tire, and work the bead back onto the rim by hand — use levers only as a last resort to avoid pinching the tube.
Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall, reinstall the wheel (reconnect the motor cable if applicable), and spin it to confirm it's true and doesn't rub anywhere.

title: Brake Pad Replacement
summary: Swap worn disc brake pads before they wear down to the metal backing.

steps.instruction: Remove the wheel next to the brake you're servicing.
Remove the small retaining pin or clip from the caliper and slide out the worn pads.
Check pad thickness — replace if less than about 1mm of friction material remains.
Use a plastic tire lever or dedicated pad-spacer tool to gently push the caliper pistons back, making room for the new, thicker pads.
Wipe the pistons and caliper clean with isopropyl alcohol. Avoid getting any oil or grease on the pads or rotor.
Slide the new pads into the caliper and reinsert the retaining pin or clip.
Reinstall the wheel, then squeeze the brake lever several times before riding to reseat the pistons against the new pads.
Test the brake at low speed in a safe area before riding normally.

title: Chain Cleaning & Lubrication
summary: A clean, well-lubed chain shifts better and lasts much longer.
toolsRequired: Chain cleaning tool or old brush

steps.instruction: Shift to the middle of the cassette so the chain is easy to access.
Apply degreaser to a rag or chain-cleaning tool and run the chain through it several times while backpedaling.
Wipe down the cassette and chainrings with a rag to remove built-up grime.
Wipe off residual degreaser with a damp rag — avoid spraying a hose directly at hub or motor bearings.
Let the chain dry completely before lubricating.
Apply one drop of lubricant to each roller while slowly backpedaling.
Let the lube penetrate for a few minutes, then wipe off all excess from the outside of the chain — excess lube just attracts dirt.

title: Basic Battery Care
summary: Simple habits that keep your e-bike battery healthy for longer.

steps.instruction: For day-to-day storage, keep the charge roughly between 20% and 80% rather than leaving it fully depleted or fully charged for long periods.
Store the battery somewhere cool and dry — avoid direct sun and freezing temperatures during extended storage.
Periodically wipe the battery contacts and mounting rails with a dry cloth to prevent corrosion or a poor connection.
Charge using only the charger supplied or specified by the bike's manufacturer.
If the bike will sit unused for more than a few weeks, charge the battery to roughly 50–60% first rather than storing it full or empty.
Stop using the battery immediately and have it inspected if you notice swelling, unusual heat, or a strange smell.

title: Motor Error Code Troubleshooting
summary: First checks to run before assuming the motor system needs a technician.

steps.instruction: Note the exact error code shown on the display — the specific number or letter combination matters, not just that an error appeared.
Power the system fully off and back on. Many transient errors, like a momentary sensor glitch, clear after a simple restart.
Check that the battery is properly seated with clean, dry contacts — a poor connection is a very common cause of 'communication error' codes.
Inspect the motor and speed-sensor cable connectors for dirt, moisture, or a partially unplugged connector.
Look up the specific code in the manufacturer's documentation or app — codes vary significantly between motor systems.

If the error persists after these checks, avoid continuing to use the motorized assist and have the system inspected by a qualified e-bike technician — motor and controller faults can be electrically hazardous to diagnose further yourself.

title: Derailleur Adjustment
summary: Fix sluggish, hunting, or noisy shifting with a limit-screw and cable-tension check.
toolsRequired: Bike stand or way to lift the rear wheel

steps.instruction: Lift or support the rear wheel so it can spin freely, and shift to the smallest rear cog.
Check the high-limit screw (usually marked H) — the derailleur should line up directly under the smallest cog. Adjust the screw if the chain rubs or won't reach it.
Shift to the largest rear cog and check the low-limit screw (marked L) similarly, making sure the chain can't jump off into the spokes.
If shifting is sluggish or hunts between gears, adjust the barrel adjuster on the derailleur or shifter in small quarter-turn increments while pedaling and shifting.
Turn the adjuster to add cable tension if the chain hesitates to shift to a larger cog, or release tension if it overshoots.
Recheck shifting across the full range of gears, fine-tuning until each shift is quick and quiet.

title: Tire Pressure Check
summary: A quick habit that improves both ride comfort and rolling efficiency.
toolsRequired: Pressure gauge (or one built into a pump)

steps.instruction: Find the recommended pressure range printed on the tire's sidewall (in PSI and/or bar).
Remove the valve cap and press the gauge firmly onto the valve to get a reading.
Compare the reading to the recommended range — lean toward the higher end for pavement and efficiency, somewhat lower (within range) for off-road grip.
Add air with a pump if low, checking the gauge periodically as you go.
If overinflated, briefly press the small pin inside the valve to release a little air, then recheck.
Replace the valve cap to keep dirt out.

title: Full Drivetrain Cleaning
summary: A deeper clean covering the cassette, chainrings, and jockey wheels, not just the chain.

steps.instruction: Shift into an easy-to-access middle gear.
Apply degreaser across the cassette, chainrings, derailleur jockey wheels, and chain.
Use a stiff brush to work degreaser into the gaps between cassette cogs and around the jockey wheels, where grime builds up most.
Wipe everything down with a clean rag, repeating with fresh degreaser on especially dirty spots.
Rinse with a damp (not high-pressure) rag to remove residual degreaser.
Dry thoroughly, then relubricate the chain (see the Chain Cleaning & Lubrication guide).
Spin the pedals and shift through the gears to confirm smooth, quiet operation.

title: Light & Display Troubleshooting
summary: Quick checks before assuming a light or display unit has actually failed.

steps.instruction: Confirm the main battery has sufficient charge — a low battery can make displays or lights behave erratically or shut off.
Check that all visible cable connectors to the display and lights are firmly seated and free of corrosion or moisture.
Power-cycle the system (fully off, wait a few seconds, then back on) to clear a possible display glitch.
If a light doesn't turn on, check whether it has its own separate battery or fuse, and confirm the bulb or LED unit isn't visibly damaged.
Check the display for a specific error code and cross-reference the manufacturer's manual.
If the issue persists after these checks, treat it as an electrical fault needing professional diagnosis rather than continuing to force resets.
